title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the setup of the transverse vibration problem for a thin elastic lamina (a cantilever beam) clamped in a wall at A, with free end at B (or F in the deflected figure). The previous page introduced the abscissa x = BX from the free end, the small deflection y = XY, the element weight K dx/k, the curvature radius r ≈ dx²/ddy for small slopes, and the bending moment K cc·ddy/dx².

§III gives the kinematics. At time t (in seconds), regard y at a fixed point as a function of t alone. The velocity of point Y along YV is dy/dt and its acceleration is d²y/dt². To express this in 'absolute measure', with gravity's acceleration as the unit, Euler divides by 2b. Here b is the distance a heavy body falls in one second, so g = 2b, since s = g t²/2 at t = 1. The accelerating force is therefore (1/2b)·d²y/dt².

§IV makes the two-variable nature explicit. y = y(x,t), and Euler adopts the bracket ('vncinulis inclusis') notation for partial derivatives. The curvature radius becomes (dx²/ddy) with x alone varying. The 'moment of elasticity', i.e. the moment needed to hold that curvature, is Kcc (∂²y/∂x²). The accelerating force (carried onto the next page) is (1/2b)(∂²y/∂t²).

The next pages equate the d'Alembert inertial forces (K dx/2bk)·y_tt with the bending moments. This yields the Euler–Bernoulli beam equation, in modern form EI y_xxxx + ρA y_tt = 0. It is solved for the clamped-free lamina, with new vibration species.
errors: None of substance. The small-slope approximations (ds ≈ dx, r ≈ dx²/y_xx) are deliberate and stated on the previous page. The factor 2b correctly converts acceleration to units of g.

ideas.what: Velocity and acceleration of a point of the vibrating lamina as time derivatives at fixed x; acceleration expressed in units of gravity via g = 2b (b = fall distance in 1 s)
ideas.modern_name: Kinematics / d'Alembert inertial force in gravitational units
ideas.where_published: Many Euler papers use the same 2b (or g = 2b) convention, e.g. in his works on vibrating strings and on fluids

ideas.what: Explicit recognition that the deflection is a function of two variables (x, t), with bracketed partial-derivative notation
ideas.modern_name: Partial derivatives / PDE formulation of beam vibration
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (bracket notation for partial derivatives, 1730s–1750s); d'Alembert and Euler for vibrating-string PDEs
ideas.where_published: Euler's vibrating-string papers (e.g. E119, E140) and Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III

ideas.what: Bending moment proportional to curvature: Kcc·y_xx
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli bending law M = EI κ
ideas.where_published: E65 (Additamentum I De curvis elasticis, 1744); E40; discussed in Truesdell's Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (Opera omnia II.11/2)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a purely set-up page. It defines velocity, acceleration in gravitational units, and the partial-derivative formulation for the beam. All of this is standard Euler material and is well documented by Truesdell.
transcription_corrections: In §IV the curvature-radius formula appears in the image as (dx²/(ddy)), consistent with the transcription.
The page signature is 'Lll 2', with the catchword 'dire-'.
